title: Shishupala
hook: Bhishma tells the hall how Shishupala was born, and why Krishna once promised his mother a hundred pardons
carry: his silence is a promise kept

segments.voice: Yesterday Shishupala's anger spread through the hall, Bhishma held Bhima back, and Krishna still hadn't moved. One long breath out first.
screen: `ANGER THAT SPREADS, ANGER THAT IS HELD.`

segments.voice: The kings are muttering about war. Bhima has nearly leapt across the hall. Bhishma has been mocked to his face. And the one person all of this is about just sits there, and hasn't said a word. So Bhishma, still holding Bhima's arm, does something unexpected. He stops the argument and tells a story. If you want to understand this hall, he says in effect, you have to go back to the day Shishupala was born.
screen: `WHY IS KRISHNA SILENT?` → `BHISHMA TELLS A STORY.` → `BACK TO THE CRADLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Bhishma tells it. Shishupala was born in the royal house of Chedi with three eyes and four arms, and he cried out at birth with a strange, unearthly cry. His frightened parents thought of giving him up. Then a voice came from no one they could see. Don't abandon him. He will grow strong. His death is not yet. And it told them how to know who would end his life: the one on whose lap the child's extra arms would fall away and his third eye would vanish. So the king and queen put the baby on the lap of every visitor. King after king held him. Nothing happened. Then Krishna came to visit his aunt, and the child was placed on his lap. The two extra arms fell away. The third eye sank into his forehead and was gone. Now his mother knew whose hand would one day take her son's life, and she was Krishna's father's sister. She begged him for a boon: spare my son. Krishna promised to pardon a hundred of Shishupala's offenses, even ones that deserved death. So that's what Krishna is doing in the hall. He isn't ignoring the insults. He's counting them. His silence is a promise to his aunt, made over a cradle long ago, kept insult by insult. Patience here isn't the absence of anger. It's a word given, and honored, even when it costs something.
screen: `THREE EYES AND FOUR ARMS.` · `A VOICE: DON'T ABANDON HIM.` · `ON KRISHNA'S LAP, THE SIGNS FALL AWAY.` · `A MOTHER ASKS, KRISHNA PROMISES.` · then, large: `HIS SILENCE IS A PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of a promise you're keeping, maybe quietly and for a long time: to call, to show up, to be patient with someone who's hard to be patient with. See the person you made it to; breathe in and feel the weight of it, breathe out and notice what keeping it has asked of you. If you pray, you can hold that promise in your prayer; if not, simply honor it in silence.
Shishupala. Born with three eyes and four arms, spared at his mother's plea, and pardoned by Krishna a hundred times by promise.
Your line: his silence is a promise kept. A hundred pardons, and he's counting. Day seven hundred sixty-one, done.

howItsDone: Some storytellers and commentators use Shishupala's birth story to explain Krishna's patience in the hall, reading his silence as the keeping of a promise to his aunt.

chat.meaning: Krishna promised his aunt, Shishupala's mother, to pardon a hundred offenses. His silence is that promise, kept insult by insult.
